profile.name: Hooping
profile.tagline: Manipulation of and artistic movement or dancing with one or multiple hoops
profile.insight: In November 2019, Jenny Doan broke the continuous hooping record by hula-hooping for 100 hours at the District Brew Yards in Chicago.
profile.profile: Hooping is the manipulation of and artistic movement or dancing with a hoop or multiple hoops made of materials like polyethylene, wood, or metal. Modern hoopers use heavier, larger diameter hoops than traditional children's toys to rotate the hoop around the waist, hips, chest, neck, and limbs. The practice combines technical moves and tricks with freestyle or technical dancing, drawing influences from flow arts, hip-hop, and rhythmic gymnastics.
profile.profile_long:
Hooping, also called hula hooping or hoop dance, is the physical dexterity activity and art form involving the manipulation of and artistic movement or dancing with one or more hoops. The practice combines technical moves and tricks with freestyle or technical dancing. Hoops can be crafted from polyethylene (HDPE), polypropylene, aluminum, wood, or polyvinyl chloride, and are often wrapped with colorful, reflective, or grip tape. In contrast to lightweight children's toys, modern adult hoopers use heavier and larger diameter hoops, typically starting at 38 to 44 inches, which allows for slower rotation and controlled movement around various parts of the body.

The history of hooping spans ancient civilizations and modern revivals. The earliest known incidence of hooping dates back to ancient Egypt around 1000 BC, where children used large hoops made of grape vines. Recreational hooping later appeared in 14th-century England, and the term 'hula' became associated with the activity in the early 19th century when British sailors observed similarities to traditional Hawaiian hula. Independently, Native Americans developed complex hoop dance traditions using multiple small hoops for storytelling. In the twentieth century, commercial manufacturing took off when Australian bamboo hoops inspired Richard P. Knerr and Arthur K. Melin to found Wham-O, leading to the massive 1958 hula hoop craze in the United States.

Today, hooping exists in numerous forms, including hoop dance, street busking, fire hooping, and LED hooping. Fire hoops incorporate spokes capped with Kevlar wicking, while LED hoops utilize internal batteries and microchips to produce visual patterns through persistence of vision. Grassroots communities gather at events like Burning Man, World Hoop Day, and regional convergences to share techniques. Furthermore, scientific studies by organizations such as the American Council on Exercise have demonstrated that hooping functions as an effective aerobic workout, improving cardiovascular health, flexibility, and core strength while burning significant calories.

Specialized sub-genres and disciplines showcase extreme human capability, ranging from endurance records exceeding 100 hours to massive group synchronizations. Whether practiced in fitness studios alongside Pilates and yoga, performed by circus artists like Elena Lev and Lisa Lottie, or celebrated through indigenous cultural heritage at the Heard Museum, hooping continues to evolve as a dynamic global movement form rooted in object manipulation and flow arts.

sections.origins_and_history: The earliest known incidence of hooping was in ancient Egypt as early as 1000 BC, where children used large hoops made of grape vines. In the 14th century, recreational hooping swept across England. The word 'hula' became associated with the toy in the early 19th century when British sailors visited the Hawaiian Islands. Independently, Native Americans developed their own traditions surrounding the Hoop Dance, utilizing up to 30 hoops in storytelling rituals. In 1957, an Australian company manufactured bamboo hoops, inspiring Wham-O founders Richard P. Knerr and Arthur K. Melin to launch the plastic hula hoop in Southern California in 1958, selling over 25 million units in four months.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Hooping combines technical moves and tricks with freestyle or technical dancing. Hoopers rotate the hoop around the waist, hips, chest, neck, shoulders, thighs, knees, arms, hands, thumbs, feet, and toes, as well as manipulating it off the body. Modern hoopers execute portal tricks, where the hooper steps through the hoop while it is still rotating. Performances often integrate elements from rhythmic gymnastics, hip-hop, freestyle dance, fire performance, twirling, and poi.
sections.music_and_instruments: Hooping can be practiced to or performed with music. Hoop buskers frequently combine hooping with singing and playing one or more musical instruments during street performances.
sections.costume_and_setting: Hoops are crafted from HDPE, polypropylene, aluminum, wood, or PVC tubing, and wrapped with colorful, decorative, or grip tape. Specialized props include fire hoops with Kevlar wicking and transparent LED hoops with internal batteries. Hooping takes place in dance studios, gyms, streets, and festivals such as Burning Man and regional hoop gatherings.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Hooping is practiced as an art form, circus skill, performance discipline, and fitness regimen. International celebrations like World Hoop Day raise money for charity and distribute hoops to communities in need, while competitive events like the Heard Museum Native American Hoop Dance competition celebrate cultural heritage.
sections.notable_figures: Notable figures in hooping include circus hoopers Elena Lev and Lisa Lottie, endurance record holders Aaron Hibbs and Jenny Doan, multiple-hoop record holder Marawa Ibrahim, and large-hoop record holder Ashrita Furman.
sections.regional_variants: The primary traditional variant is the Native American Hoop Dance, which focuses on rapid movements and the construction of intricate body formations representing animals like the butterfly, eagle, snake, and coyote using small hoops.
sections.lineage: Modern hooping has been influenced by art forms such as rhythmic gymnastics, hip-hop, freestyle dance, fire performance, twirling, poi, and indigenous American dance traditions.

basic_steps: rotating the hoop around the waist
rotating the hoop around the hips
stepping through the rotating hoop in a portal trick
teaching.level_notes: Beginners typically begin with a larger, heavier hoop of approximately 38-44 inches diameter to learn skills quickly, advancing to smaller 30-36 inch hoops as skill improves.

movement_profile.arms_and_hands: rotate the hoop around parts of the body other than the waist, including the hips, chest, neck, shoulders, thighs, knees, arms, hands, thumbs, feet, and toes
movement_profile.hips_and_torso: rotate the hoop around the waist and hips

signature_moves.name: Portal trick
signature_moves.description: Stepping through the hoop while it is still rotating around the body

movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Any skill where fire is a component risks injury to the person doing it.
